questions.prompt: How does this chapter define drill?
choices: Isolating a rate-determining weakness and attacking it directly
Breaking every skill into as many pieces as possible
Repeating the whole task until the weakest part fixes itself

explanation.gentle: Young defines drill as isolating the weakness that is setting the pace for the larger skill and attacking it directly.
explanation.direct: A is correct because the chapter's definition centers on targeted attack against a rate-determining weakness, not generic decomposition or passive repetition.
explanation.competitive: The move is bottleneck assault, not endless chopping or blind repetition.

questions.prompt: Why can whole-task practice be too blunt in this chapter?
choices: Because one weak point may keep limiting the whole performance
Because full-task practice is always useless
Because drills are easier than integrated learning

explanation.gentle: If one subskill is slowing everything else, broad repetition can keep missing the part that matters most.
explanation.direct: A captures the chapter's bottleneck logic: total repetitions may distribute effort too widely when one limiter is setting the pace.
explanation.competitive: Grinding the whole routine does not help much if the choke point still owns the result.

questions.prompt: Claire keeps getting slowed by the analysis section of her reports. What best follows the chapter?
choices: Create short analysis-only drills and then return to full reports
Ignore the analysis section and just finish more full reports
Study unrelated report templates until the weakness disappears

explanation.gentle: The chapter would isolate the weak subskill that is slowing the larger task and target it directly.
explanation.direct: A follows drill by pulling out the rate-determining weakness for concentrated practice before reintegration.
explanation.competitive: Hit the bottleneck instead of doing another full lap around the same stall point.

questions.prompt: What makes an isolated drill worth doing?
choices: It targets the weakness that truly limits the whole skill
It feels neat and easy to measure
It removes the need to return to the full task

explanation.gentle: A drill matters when it isolates the part that is actually holding the larger performance back.
explanation.direct: A is correct because the chapter justifies isolation through leverage, not convenience or permanent fragmentation.
explanation.competitive: The fragment earns time only if it is the weak link, not if it just looks tidy in the log.

questions.prompt: Noor is unsure whether a guitar fragment is the real bottleneck or just easy to practice alone. What question does the chapter push her to ask?
choices: Does this fragment truly constrain the whole performance?
Can I make this fragment even cleaner before playing the song again?
Should I avoid the full song until the fragment feels perfect?

explanation.gentle: The chapter asks whether the isolated piece is rate-determining or merely convenient.
explanation.direct: A fits the chapter's boundary on drill: diagnose leverage rather than choosing the easiest fragment.
explanation.competitive: The real question is whether this piece owns the result or just flatters the practice session.

questions.prompt: What role does reintegration play in drill?
choices: It tests whether the isolated gain improves the whole skill
It replaces the need for any diagnosis
It proves that full-task practice no longer matters

explanation.gentle: Reintegration shows whether the work done in isolation actually helps the larger performance.
explanation.direct: A states the chapter's safeguard: the drill has to come back into the integrated task and change it there.
explanation.competitive: Put the sharpened piece back in the machine and see whether the output improves.

questions.prompt: Maya isolates one pronunciation pattern before returning to full dialogue practice. Why does that match the chapter?
choices: Because one weak pattern is distorting the whole exchange
Because drills should replace conversation practice permanently
Because pronunciation is always the only thing worth practicing

explanation.gentle: The chapter supports isolation when one weak point keeps slowing an otherwise integrated performance.
explanation.direct: A follows drill because the pronunciation issue is being treated as the rate-determining weakness, then returned to the larger task.
explanation.competitive: She is attacking the sound that keeps wrecking the chain, not fleeing the conversation forever.

questions.prompt: When does drill start to drift away from the chapter's logic?
choices: When the learner isolates a convenient fragment that is not truly rate-determining
When the learner spends any time practicing a part separately
When the learner checks the whole task again after the drill

explanation.gentle: Drift begins when the isolated work no longer targets the weakness that actually constrains the larger skill.
explanation.direct: A is right because the chapter warns against choosing fragments for neatness instead of leverage.
explanation.competitive: The drift starts when the side piece is polished for comfort while the real choke point stays in charge.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter still keep the whole task central even after introducing drills?
choices: Because the real skill is integrated and the drill must serve that whole performance
Because drill is mainly a motivational trick
Because the isolated piece matters more than the whole skill

explanation.gentle: Young uses isolated work to help the whole skill, not to replace the whole skill.
explanation.direct: A fits the chapter because drill is a temporary precision move inside integrated performance.
explanation.competitive: The pieces matter only because the full chain still has to survive.

questions.prompt: After the learner has attacked the bottleneck directly, what question naturally follows?
choices: What signals will show whether the change is really working?
How can the task be broken into even more pieces forever?
How can the learner avoid returning to the full performance?

explanation.gentle: Once the weak point has been targeted, the learner needs clearer information about whether the larger performance is improving.
explanation.direct: A is the right bridge because the next concern is the quality of feedback coming from results after the drill.
explanation.competitive: After you hit the choke point, you need harsher signals from the field.
